answer:
The job ran and finished on emerald:mock, which is IQM's free test version of Emerald. Job ID: 01a16488-7b4a-7268-9acc-94d74d018999. The job held 4 circuits with 250 shots each and cost 0 credits.

What I ran: I used all 54 Emerald qubits, one for each atom. Every qubit started at 0, which means spin up. The real Emerald currently lists 85 CZ couplers, so I used those 85. The mock lists 90 couplers, and it contains all 85 real ones. I left out the 5 extra mock couplers. One time step is a sideways kick RX(theta) on every qubit, then the coupling exp(i pi/4 ZZ) on every coupler. I built that coupling as exactly one CZ gate per coupler. The single-qubit Z turns that come with it were folded into the phase of the next kick. I sent native gates straight to the server, so no compiler step added, merged, or removed any coupler gate. I read the circuits back from the server. Each circuit has 255 CZ gates, which is 85 couplers times 3 steps, and each coupler appears exactly 3 times. Each circuit measures QB1 to QB54. In each bitstring, the first character is QB1 and the last is QB54.

The ideal numbers come from an exact noise-free simulation of the circuits I submitted. Each qubit's result depends only on qubits within 2 couplers of it, so I simulated each of those small groups exactly. I checked that method against a full simulation on a 12-qubit patch of the chip. The magnetization is the average of Z over all 54 qubits. Z is +1 for up (bit 0) and -1 for down (bit 1).

Results, ideal against measured:
- theta = 0: ideal 1.000, measured 0.004
- theta = 0.2 pi: ideal 0.452, measured -0.027
- theta = 0.35 pi: ideal 0.113, measured 0.023
- theta = 0.5 pi: ideal 0.000, measured -0.016

What a perfect quantum computer would show: with no sideways field, every spin stays up and the magnetization stays at 1. The couplings only add phases, so they cannot flip a spin by themselves. A weak field of 0.2 pi tips the spins, and the couplings then spread that disorder through the sheet. After 3 steps the magnetization falls to about 0.45. A field of 0.35 pi drops it to about 0.11. At 0.5 pi the ordered state is gone and the magnetization is 0. The principle is that a stronger sideways field melts the order faster. The spins tangle with their neighbors, so the sheet loses its shared direction.

What the mock shows: all 4 measured values are near 0, even at theta = 0. That happens because the mock device returns made-up bits that do not depend on the circuit. The mock proves that the circuits are valid and accepted on Emerald's layout. It cannot show the physics. To see the melting curve in real data, the same job would have to run on the real Emerald, and that costs credits.
